product.name: L-Carnitine — Cellular Energy Transport
product.description:
L-carnitine is an amino acid-derived quaternary ammonium compound studied in laboratory research for its role in cellular energy metabolism and mitochondrial fatty-acid transport. Research investigations commonly examine carnitine-dependent transport of long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane, acyl-group homeostasis, and downstream biochemical processes associated with mitochondrial substrate utilization and cellular bioenergetics.

This material is supplied as a liquid research solution for analytical testing, biochemical pathway studies, stability evaluation, and other non-clinical laboratory research applications.

For Research Use Only (RUO). Not for human or animal use.
product.compoundClass: Amino Acid–Derived Quaternary Ammonium Compound (Trimethylammonium Betaine)
product.sequence: Not applicable — small-molecule compound, not a peptide (no amino acid sequence)
product.technicalOverview:
L-carnitine (levocarnitine) is the naturally occurring (R)-enantiomer of carnitine, a small quaternary ammonium compound synthesized endogenously from the amino acids lysine and methionine and also obtained from dietary intake. It is not a peptide — the molecule is a single small-molecule zwitterion, which is why this listing carries no amino acid sequence.

Its central, well-established role is as an obligate cofactor of the carnitine shuttle: it conjugates with long-chain fatty acyl-CoA esters via carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT1) at the outer mitochondrial membrane, is translocated across the inner membrane by carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase, and is reconverted to acyl-CoA by carnitine palmitoyltransferase II (CPT2) for beta-oxidation. This CPT1/translocase/CPT2 shuttle is the rate-limiting step controlling how much long-chain fat a cell can oxidize, which is why acylcarnitine profiles — not free carnitine alone — are the standard readout in mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation research.

Beyond fatty-acid transport, carnitine buffers the mitochondrial acyl-CoA/free-CoA ratio: exporting excess acyl groups as acylcarnitines keeps free CoA available for other mitochondrial reactions, including pyruvate dehydrogenase flux. This buffering role is mechanistically well supported in vitro; broader extrapolations to exercise performance or fat loss in humans are considerably weaker and should be read as hypotheses rather than established results — the human supplementation literature on those outcomes is mixed.

The compound was historically termed vitamin BT after the mealworm (Tenebrio molitor) growth assay that first identified it as an essential factor for that organism. The name is a misnomer for humans and other higher organisms, which biosynthesize their own carnitine and do not require a dietary source under normal conditions.

Cellular bioenergetics and substrate-utilization research in isolated mitochondria and cell culture

product.storageHandling: Supplied as a liquid solution. Store tightly sealed at 2–8°C, protected from light. L-carnitine solutions are generally stable under refrigeration, but avoid repeated freeze-thaw cycles and prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures. Inspect for precipitation or discoloration before use and discard if present.
